transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-20 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Rachel Owens (SummitBridge Head of Data), Mark Saito (Platform Eng), Priya Nair (Dir Security)

Summary: Walkthrough of Redwood Console per-route usage and cost. Focus on how to attribute spend to product routes, how routing policies and dedicated capacity affect unit cost, and operational controls for security and audits.

Topics covered:
- Per-route dashboards and lenses
- Cost breakdown (token-level, route-level, model variant cost)
- Batching/caching knobs and expected impact
- Dedicated vs Hosted routing tradeoffs
- Security: SOC2, KMS, audit logs, VPC

Transcript start:
[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood. Diego and I will run through the console and cost playbook. How's the audio?
[00:00:07] Rachel Owens: Sounds good, Maya. Thanks. We've got Mark and Priya on from infra and security. I'm Rachel, I run data and ML infra here.
[00:00:12] Mark Saito: Hey all.
[00:00:15] Priya Nair: Hi.
[00:00:17] Diego Alvarez: Awesome. I'll share my screen in a sec, showing the Console. Quick ask up front — what's the most important success metric for a pilot? Cost per request, latency, or data isolation?
[00:00:28] Rachel Owens: Uh, primarily cost per user request and predictable latency SLAs. We have regulatory concerns so data residency and audit logs matter too.
[00:00:35] Maya Chen: Great. We'll hit all those. Diego, you can jump in on the dashboard and show route attribution.
[00:00:40] Diego Alvarez: Yep — sharing now. (screen) Alright, this is the Project view — you can see route cards for the main product endpoints. For SummitBridge we would map each API route to a "route" in Redwood — that lets you get per-route token breakdowns and cost.
[00:00:55] Diego Alvarez: So for example this route, /transactions/classify, you get token counts, avg latency, and then a cost column which is model * tokens * model unit price. Note — our price in the Console reflects your contract, but this is the example ballpark.
[00:01:14] Rachel Owens: Quick Q — does the console do attribution for composite workflows? Like when you fan out across models and do a re-ranker?
[00:01:22] Diego Alvarez: Yeah, good question. We stitch spans of a single request; the console breaks down per-subcall. For composite pipelines we show both per-call and aggregate route-level totals so you can see the re-ranker cost as a line item.
[00:01:36] Mark Saito: Is that based on trace IDs we push or automatic?
[00:01:39] Diego Alvarez: We support both. If you push trace IDs via headers we can tie them; otherwise the SDK generates an internal correlation id. There's occasional mismatch if customers do edge-caching but we surface suspected duplicates as suspected double counts.
[00:01:54] Priya Nair: About PII — we need to know what data leaves our VPC. How detailed are the audit logs?
[00:02:01] Maya Chen: We can export request/response hashes, timestamps, model variant used, and route names. Full responses can be redacted per config — and in Private deployments you can keep everything customer-side. We'll send the SOC2 pack after.
[00:02:14] Rachel Owens: Private would be ideal but we might start with a dedicated pool. Any numbers around latency uplift when going Dedicated?
[00:02:22] Diego Alvarez: Dedicated tends to reduce tail latency variance — think 5–15% improvement on p95 depending on the model and sequence lengths. Also you get predictable throughput. But cost per token can be higher unless you commit reserved capacity.
[00:02:36] Maya Chen: And that's where the Optimize recommendations come in — Diego will show batching and caching knobs that reduce effective unit cost on Dedicated.
[00:02:45] Diego Alvarez: Jumping to the Optimize tab — here we surface intelligent batching recommendations per route. For example this route had a lot of short prompts, we suggested reducing the max batch size and enabling prefix KV caching to get a 18% token reduction in practice.
[00:03:02] Rachel Owens: Wait, prefix KV caching — our platform uses big stateful sessions, is that compatible?
[00:03:08] Diego Alvarez: Yes, the KV cache is session-aware. You can opt-in by route or globally, and we maintain eviction policies. There is a caveat when you have multi-region routing; caches are per-region unless you enable a cross-region sync which we don't recommend for low-latency workloads.
[00:03:24] Mark Saito: Related — we need to know how the Console attributes cost when a request falls back to a smaller model in a canary or fallback policy.
[00:03:31] Diego Alvarez: We show the actual model that served each token. If you have a fallback, the cost is charged according to served model; the Console lets you filter by fallback reason so you can find capacity pressure fallbacks.
[00:03:43] Rachel Owens: Can we set cost alerts per route?
[00:03:45] Maya Chen: Yep — set threshold alerts by daily cost, by unexpected spike delta, or by per-token average. Many customers set an anomaly alert and a hard daily cap for sandbox routes.
[00:03:55] Priya Nair: On encryption — are keys customer-managed?
[00:03:58] Maya Chen: For Private deployments yes. For Dedicated we offer KMS integration with customer-managed keys for request metadata and model artifacts. You can also integrate with HSM for stricter key policies.
[00:04:09] Mark Saito: For the pilot we're thinking about 3 routes: classify, enrichment, and summarization. What would be your recommended default model mix to keep costs low?
[00:04:18] Diego Alvarez: A common pattern: use a smaller encoder model for embeddings/enrichment (quantized 4-bit for cost), a mid-tier generative model for classify, and a more powerful model only for summarize when length warrants. And then use reranking only for a small top-k. That reduces total tokens served.
[00:04:36] Rachel Owens: Could you demo the per-route cost drilldown?
[00:04:38] Diego Alvarez: Yep — clicking into /summarize route... (pause) Here you see hourly token trend, percentile latencies, and column for cost breakdown: model compute, storage for KV-cache, and network egress. We attach annotations for model changes and deploy rollouts so you can correlate cost bumps.
[00:04:58] Maya Chen: Note — the storage line is usually small except for heavy KV cache usage; we call that out so it's not a surprise.
[00:05:05] Rachel Owens: I see a "Shared vs Dedicated" cost view — how does shared hosted pricing compare if we have seasonal spikes?
[00:05:11] Diego Alvarez: Hosted is OPEX metered and helps with spikes because the underlying infra autos-scales. Dedicated gives you predictability and isolation, but you either reserve or pay for burst capacity. Many teams start hosted for spike management then move to a hybrid where common routes run on Dedicated and burst to Hosted via routing policies.
[00:05:29] Mark Saito: That hybrid routing — is it automatic?
[00:05:31] Diego Alvarez: You configure routing policies by route — priority, latency target, and failover model. There's also an automatic fallback policy option that uses capacity thresholds to fail to hosted. We can demo that in the pilot.
[00:05:41] Priya Nair: For audits we need immutable logs for 12 months. Can Redwood export immutable logs to our S3?
[00:05:47] Maya Chen: Yes, we support log sinks to S3 with timestamped objects and checksum verification. For Private, logs never leave your VPC. We'll include the retention and immutability options in the SOC2 package we send.
[00:05:58] Rachel Owens: Ok — let's talk cost playbook. If we see a 25% month-over-month increase in token spend, what's the playbook?
[00:06:06] Diego Alvarez: Step 1: identify routes driving the spend with the per-route lens. Step 2: run Optimize recommendations — batch tuning, prefix caching, model quantization suggestions. Step 3: use canary rollouts to migrate to a cheaper variant and monitor quality regressions via our eval hooks. Step 4: if still high, introduce sampling or rate limits on non-critical routes.
[00:06:26] Rachel Owens: Eval hooks — can you explain?
[00:06:28] Diego Alvarez: Eval hooks let you run golden prompt sets against model variants on deploy. You get automatic quality delta alerts. Many customers gate cost-driven rollouts behind a quality threshold.
[00:06:38] Mark Saito: For the pilot, can we set up the eval set to mirror production traffic?
[00:06:41] Diego Alvarez: Yes, you can upload a sample set. If you send us a representative CSV we can import and run the eval template. That ties back to Diego's action item to provide a runbook.
[00:06:51] Rachel Owens: Do you have examples of cost savings customers have seen?
[00:06:54] Maya Chen: One fintech customer saw a 30% reduction after batching + prefix caching and moving enrichment to a quantized embedding model. Another moved to hybrid routing to avoid peak egress charges. We'll include an anonymized case study.
[00:07:06] Priya Nair: Anything we should be aware of in terms of data residency when we use hosted?
[00:07:10] Maya Chen: Hosted lets you pick region endpoints; we have EU, NA, APAC regions. For strict residency Private is the path.
[00:07:17] Mark Saito: Can you show the exportable CSV with route-level cost?
[00:07:20] Diego Alvarez: Sure — export button here. (pause) The CSV includes timestamp, route, model, tokens_in, tokens_out, model_cost, network_cost, cache_storage_cost. We can add custom columns like internal product id if you forward it in headers.
[00:07:38] Rachel Owens: Great — we'll use that to map to our billing.
[00:07:40] Maya Chen: Quick demo of anomaly detection — this uses baseline windows and flags deviations. You can tune sensitivity per route.
[00:07:48] Diego Alvarez: Also, the Console annotates rollout events. If you deploy a new model and see a cost jump, the annotation helps root cause quickly.
[00:07:57] Rachel Owens: About the pilot — what's a minimal pilot scope?
[00:08:00] Maya Chen: We usually recommend 2–4 routes, 2 weeks of baseline collection, then a 4–6 week pilot with an SLO for latency and cost. That gives enough data to tune batching and caching.
[00:08:11] Mark Saito: For pricing we need an estimate for 100k requests/day with mixed payload sizes.
[00:08:16] Maya Chen: We'll share a Dedicated pricing sheet, but I can give a back-of-envelope: with hybrid routing and quantization we often reduce unit costs by 20–35% vs naive hosted defaults. We'll send a modeled spreadsheet with your routes once we get the sample CSV.
[00:08:30] Priya Nair: Security checklist for procurement — SSO, RBAC, SOC2, ISO, encryption, logging. Anything else?
[00:08:37] Maya Chen: Third-party penetration test reports and our vendor SSP. We'll attach that pack. For SSO we support SAML and OIDC, role-based access and fine-grained API keys per route.
[00:08:49] Rachel Owens: One more — how often do you roll quantized kernels and could they change latency characteristics?
[00:08:55] Diego Alvarez: We continuously add optimized kernels; we publish performance profiles per model+quantization. Sometimes you see minor p95 shifts, which is why we recommend evals and canary rollouts.
[00:09:05] Mark Saito: If we need dedicated on-prem later, how hard is migration?
[00:09:09] Maya Chen: We offer a Private package that includes a customer-managed control plane. App-level configs and routes map 1:1, but you'll need to provision hardware; our engineering team helps with onboarding. Migration work typically takes 6–10 weeks depending on scale.
[00:09:21] Rachel Owens: Ok looks good. Can you run through the exact pilot deliverables?
[00:09:25] Diego Alvarez: Sure — pilot deliverables: 1) baseline telemetry collection for 2 weeks, 2) run Optimize recommendations and implement batching/caching where safe, 3) run evals against fallback variants, 4) cost/latency report at end with recommended long-term routing.
[00:09:40] Maya Chen: We'll add an acceptance criteria doc — typically <5% quality delta on eval set and target cost reduction.
[00:09:48] Rachel Owens: Sounds reasonable. Priya — anything else from security?
[00:09:51] Priya Nair: We'd like the SOC2 and KMS integration docs and a network diagram. Also, confirm RBAC for keys and audit retention.
[00:09:59] Maya Chen: We'll send the SOC2 pack and network diagram.
[00:10:03] Mark Saito: For the sample CSV, we'll include columns: timestamp, route, payload_length, user_id_hash, product_id. Is that sufficient?
[00:10:11] Diego Alvarez: That's ideal. Please indicate which columns may contain PII and we'll mask on ingestion.
[00:10:17] Rachel Owens: Timeline-wise, we want to turn a pilot on in December and have exec review mid-Jan.
[00:10:22] Maya Chen: Great — we'll aim to get docs and pricing over by Monday.
[00:10:26] Diego Alvarez: I'll attach the benchmark runbook and a sample prompt set template.
[00:10:30] Rachel Owens: Perfect.
[00:10:32] Maya Chen: Any other questions?
[00:10:34] Priya Nair: One — do you support VPC peering for Private control plane?
[00:10:38] Maya Chen: Yes, for Private we can peer or deploy inside customer network. For Dedicated we support private endpoints and transit VPCs.
[00:10:46] Rachel Owens: Ok that's all. Thanks.
[00:10:49] Diego Alvarez: Quick note — one optimization we didn't demo live is sampling non-critical routes down to a smaller model and using a confidence threshold to route to full model only when needed. That often yields big wins.
[00:11:00] Maya Chen: Cool. We'll wrap with a recap.
[00:11:02] Maya Chen: Recap: 1) Maya to share Dedicated pricing and SOC2 pack by 2026-11-23. 2) Diego to send benchmark/runbook and sample prompts by 2026-11-25. 3) Mark to provide route CSV + PII annotations by 2026-11-24. 4) Schedule 30-min pilot scoping for week of Nov 30.
[00:11:23] Rachel Owens: Confirmed. Thanks Maya, Diego.
[00:11:26] Mark Saito: Thanks.
[00:11:27] Priya Nair: Bye.
[00:11:28] Diego Alvarez: Thanks everyone.
[00:11:30] Maya Chen: Bye — we'll follow up via email with links.
[00:11:33] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-hears for technical terms (e.g., "KV cash" instead of "KV cache"), timestamps approximate.

Referenced artifacts/links: Dedicated pricing (link to internal sheet), SOC2 pack (link), benchmark runbook template (link), sample CSV template (link).
